text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- When aeroplanes come too close in midair, 77 percent of cases are due to human error. Last year there was about seven close shaves a month in Swedish skies, often over Stockholm, according to a new state report.

- The public sector is overrepresented in the number of complaints to the discrimination ombudsman (DO). From 27 complaints received by the DO about racial discrimation more than half come from the public sector.

- Car safety equipment maker Autoliv posted a three percent rise in sales although volumes of goods sold rose by nine percent in the first half of 1997. This was due to a combination of a stronger U.S. dollar and price pressure. U.S. sales accounted for 34 percent of total sales.

- Tax income from tobacco products is now only expected to reach 7.2 billion crowns which is two billion crowns below estimates last autumn. This is due to reduced sales that could be due to people giving up smoking or to buying cigarettes that have no tax. Advertisements offering cheap imported cigarettes. are being investigated.

- The association against advertisements for children under 12 is not working as it only controls those concerning goods, such as toys, but other products, such as sugar coated breakfast cereals, can be directed at children.

- Head of Autoliv, Gunnar Bark, said he was satisfied with the car safety equipment maker's performance in the first half of 1997. Sales rose three percent to June 30 to $1.68 billion of which airbags accounted for $1.21 billion.

- The OMX index of the Stockholm bourse has soared 84 percent in the past year, ahead of other world bourses. The U.S. has seen an 82 percent lift and the Netherlands 83 percent. The OMX index tracks the 30 most traded shares. The biggest risers over the year were Nokia, up 159 percent, Ericsson rising 146 percent and Nordbanken 116 percent.

- Car safety equipment group Autoliv Inc posted a slightly higher than expected profit of $177 million against $161 million a year ago despite the strengthening of the U.S. dollar. This was largely due to better than expected U.S. sales. The share rose 2.5 crowns and ended at 295.50 crowns in Stockholm.

- Petrol consumption is continuing to fall despite positive signs in the economy. In the first half of 1997 consumption fell by 35 million litres, according to preliminary figures from Statistics Sweden. If this rate of decrease continues, by the end of the year consumption will be at its lowest in nine years at about 5,468 million litres.
